Phrases & Idioms.question: ১) To catch a tartar
Phrases & Idioms.option1: ক) To trap wanted criminal with great difficulty
Phrases & Idioms.option2: খ) To catch a dangerous person
Phrases & Idioms.option4: ঘ) To deal with a person who is more than one's match
Phrases & Idioms.exp:
Catch a tartar - To attack or oppose someone too strong for one.
- Collins Dictionary

Phrases & Idioms.question: ২) To drive home
Phrases & Idioms.option2: খ) To return to place of rest
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To drive home: give special importance or value to.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৩) To have an axe to grind
Phrases & Idioms.option1: ক) A private end to serve
Phrases & Idioms.option2: খ) To fail to arouse interest
Phrases & Idioms.option4: ঘ) To work for both sides
Phrases & Idioms.exp:
Axe to grind means to have a selfish reason for saying or doing something. Like doing something with vested interests.
Usage: People who don't have an axe to grind will offer you the best opinion.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৪) A close shave
Phrases & Idioms.exp: A close shave: a narrow escape from danger or disaster.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৫) To end in smoke
Phrases & Idioms.exp: It means fall short, fall through, fall to the ground, come to nothing, end in smoke, fail, miscarry.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৬) To keep one's head
Phrases & Idioms.option1: ক) To be agile and active
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To keep one's head : to remain calm and sensible when in an awkward situation that might cause a person to panic or go out of control.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৭) To pick holes
Phrases & Idioms.option1: ক) To find some reason to quarrel
Phrases & Idioms.option4: ঘ) To cut some part of an item
Phrases & Idioms.exp:
To point out the flaws in some thing or to criticize someone
for example : I always used to pick holes in the School Bus seats

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৮) To cross swords
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To cross swords: to quarrel or argue with someone.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৯) To beg the question
Phrases & Idioms.exp:
Beg the question
English meaning:
1. (of a fact or action) raise a point that has not been dealt with; invite an obvious question.
2.  Assume the truth of an argument or proposition to be proved, without arguing it.

Taken for granted - to believe that something is true without checking or thinking about it.

সুতরাং, বুঝা যাচ্ছে, beg the question এর অর্থ to take for granted.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ১০) Hobson's choice
Phrases & Idioms.option2: খ) Accept or leave the offer
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Hobson's choice: free choice in which only one thing is offered.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ১১) A black sheep
Phrases & Idioms.option3: গ) A partner who takes no share of the profits
Phrases & Idioms.exp: In the English language, 'Black sheep' is an idiom used to describe an odd or disreputable member of a group, especially within a family.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ১২) To fly off the handle
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To fly off the handle: lose one's temper suddenly and unexpectedly

Phrases & Idioms.question: ১৩) A man of straw
Phrases & Idioms.option1: ক) A man of no substance
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Straw means no exitance of rationality. So correct meaning of this that a man having nothing in him.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ১৪) To read between the lines
Phrases & Idioms.option4: ঘ) To grasp the hidden meaning
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To read between the lines: look for or discover a meaning that is implied rather than explicitly stated.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ১৫) To smell a rat
Phrases & Idioms.option1: ক) To see signs of plague epidemic
Phrases & Idioms.option2: খ) To get bad small of a bad dead rat
Phrases & Idioms.option4: ঘ) To be in a bad mood
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To smell a rat is often used to describe the suspicion of foul dealings because rats are related to foul and bad meanings.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ১৬) To drink like a fish
Phrases & Idioms.option4: ঘ) To drink in the company of others
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To drink like a fish: Consume large amounts of alcoholic beverages.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ১৭) I met him after a long time, but he gave me the cold shoulder.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: It's simple because in the line itself describes that he gave me cold shoulder means he ignored me it's so simple you foolish, idiot, mad, stupid, you have all given wrong answers so just get the hell out of here.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ১৮) Hush money
Phrases & Idioms.option3: গ) Money earned by wrong means
Phrases & Idioms.option4: ঘ) Bribe paid to secure silence
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Hush money: money paid to someone to prevent them from disclosing embarrassing or discreditable information.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ১৯) In the armed forces, it is considered a great privilege to die in harness.
Phrases & Idioms.option1: ক) die on a horse back
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Harness means- Engaged in one's usual routine of work. After his illness he longed to get back in harness.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ২০) Castles in the air
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Castles in the air: Dreams, hopes, or plans that are impossible, unrealistic, or have very little chance of succeeding.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ২১) The cricket match proved to be a big draw.
Phrases & Idioms.option4: ঘ) a game without any result
Phrases & Idioms.exp: According to Oxford Advanced learner's Dictionary 'Draw' refers to attract or interest sb. So here a huge attraction is the right answer.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ২২) A red letter day
Phrases & Idioms.exp: A red letter day: any day of special significance or opportunity.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ২৩) He was undecided. He let the grass grow under his feet.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Loiter means to linger about, to walk slowly.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ২৪) A baker's dozen
Phrases & Idioms.exp: A baker's dozen: from the former bakers' custom of adding an extra loaf to a dozen sold

Phrases & Idioms.question: ২৫) I am afraid he is burning the candle at both ends and ruining his life.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To work very hard and stay up very late at night.(One end of the candle is work done in the daylight, and the other end is work done at night).

Phrases & Idioms.question: ২৬) To carry the coal to Newcastle
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To carry the coal to Newcastle: to do something unnecessary.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ২৭) He is out and out a reactionary.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Out and out means in every respect or completely

Phrases & Idioms.question: ২৮) Why must you look a gift horse in the mouth?
Phrases & Idioms.option2: খ) find fault with a gift
Phrases & Idioms.exp: The proverb refers to the practice of evaluating the age of a horse by looking at its teeth. This practice is also the source of the expression 'long in the tooth', meaning old.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ২৯) Swan-song
Phrases & Idioms.option1: ক) Music as sweet as a song of birds
Phrases & Idioms.option2: খ) A melodious song in praise of someone
Phrases & Idioms.option3: গ) Praise of a woman by her lover
Phrases & Idioms.option4: ঘ) Last work of a poet or musician before death
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Swan-song: the final performance or activity of a person's career.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৩০) He is leaving the country for a good.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: For a good means forever.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৩১) To keep the wolf away from the door
Phrases & Idioms.option1: ক) To keep away from extreme poverty
Phrases & Idioms.option2: খ) To keep off an unwanted and undesirable person
Phrases & Idioms.option4: ঘ) To hold the difficulties and dangers in check
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To keep the wolf away from the door: to have sufficient money to prevent starvation or hunger.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৩২) The accounts of the murder made her flesh creep.
Phrases & Idioms.exp:
Make somebody's flesh crawl/creep:
If someone or something makes your flesh creep, you think they are extremely unpleasant or frightening.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৩৩) To break the ice
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To break the ice: do or say something to relieve tension or get conversation going in a strained situation or when strangers meet.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৩৪) I felt like a fish out of water among all those business tycoons.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To feel awkward because you are in an situation which you have not experienced before or because you are very different from the people around you.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৩৫) To bear the palm
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To bear the palm: To win reward.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৩৬) I am sure they will fight tooth and nail for their rights.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: It means fighting others with all your strength

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৩৭) To pay off old scores
Phrases & Idioms.option3: গ) To repay the old loan
Phrases & Idioms.exp: To pay off old scores: To have one's revenge.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৩৮) The question of abolition of private property is still a moot point.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Moot point means controversial point, undecided point.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৩৯) The time is running out, you must look sharp.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Look sharp means 'be quick', so 'make haste' is in order.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৪০) There is no hard and fast rule regarding this subject.
Phrases & Idioms.option2: খ) rule that is fat changing
Phrases & Idioms.option3: গ) rule that cannot be broken or modified
Phrases & Idioms.option4: ঘ) rule that can be broken or modified
Phrases & Idioms.exp: The Hard and fast rule means 'not fixed' that's why answer D rule that can be broken or modified.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৪১) The speaker gave a bird's eye view of the political conditions in the country.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Birds eye view means a situation which is viewed from high altitude or from a certain distance and from such height we can see a generalized view. That's why a general view is the correct option.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৪২) There has been bad blood between the two communities even before shouting.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: No explanation added.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৪৩) The prince did not take after the king.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Take after means resemble.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৪৪) It is high time that India did something about the population problem.
Phrases & Idioms.exp:
(it’s) high time meaning and examples -
used for saying that something should be done soon, because it is already past the time when it should have been done.
- It’s high time we got a pay rise!

(it is) past the time when something should have happened:
- It’s high time you got that bad knee looked at by a doctor!

used to say it is time to do something that should have been done a long time ago.
- It's high time we made some changes around here.

Source: Cambridge, MacMillan and Merriam-Webster dictionary.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৪৫) The dacoit murdered the man in cold blood.
Phrases & Idioms.exp:
Cold-blooded/In cold blood means 'Showing no feelings or pity for other people'.
In cold blood or Cold blooded means - Without emotion or pity; deliberately cruel or callous; without feeling or mercy; ruthlessly.
Oxford Dictionary.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৪৬) There was no opposition to the new policy by the rank and file of the Government.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: No explanation added.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৪৭) The class could not keep a straight face on hearing the strange pronunciation of the new teacher.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Keeping a straight face means remaining serious!

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৪৮) The authorities took him to task for his negligence.
Phrases & Idioms.exp: Reprimand means to tell someone formally that they have done something wrong.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৪৯) A green horn
Phrases & Idioms.exp: A green horn: an inexperienced or naive person.

Phrases & Idioms.question: ৫০) A cock and bull story
Phrases & Idioms.option4: ঘ) A foolish and concocted story
Phrases & Idioms.exp: A cock and bull story: an implausible story used as an explanation or excuse
